name: Mahayana Buddhism
era: From about the 1st century BCE to today
line: Wake up for the sake of everyone, and practise kindness as if nothing were separate.

quote.text: For as long as space endures, and for as long as living beings remain, until then may I too abide to dispel the misery of the world.
quote.source: A Guide to the Bodhisattva’s Way of Life 10.55, trans. Stephen Batchelor

quotes.text: Form is emptiness, emptiness is form.
quotes.source: Prajnaparamita Hridaya, in its common English rendering

quotes.text: Because all living beings are sick, therefore I am sick.
quotes.source: The Vimalakirti Sutra, chapter 5, trans. Burton Watson

quotes.text: All the joy the world contains has come through wishing happiness for others. All the misery the world contains has come through wanting pleasure for oneself.
quotes.source: The Way of the Bodhisattva 8.129, trans. Padmakara Translation Group

quotes.text: Beings are numberless; I vow to save them.
quotes.source: Recited daily in East Asian temples; a common English version

quotes.text: As a lamp, a cataract, a star in space, an illusion, a dewdrop, a bubble, a dream, a cloud, a flash of lightning: view all created things like this.

words.usage: The name the movement gave itself: a vehicle large enough to carry everyone to awakening.
One who vows to become a buddha in order to free all beings, and stays in the world to help.
The wish to wake up for the sake of others. Everything in the Mahayana starts from it.
The wish that others be free of suffering, joined to the will to do something about it.
Seeing how things actually are: changing, dependent and without a fixed core.
Nothing exists by itself, apart from causes, parts and the mind that names it. It does not mean that nothing exists.
One of the six qualities a bodhisattva trains in: giving, ethics, patience, effort, meditation and wisdom.
The first perfection. Giving things, giving safety and giving the teaching.
Bearing harm and hardship without anger. Shantideva gives it his longest chapter.
Teaching and helping in whatever way fits the person. The Lotus Sutra’s great theme.
The teaching that every being already has the capacity to awaken. In Chinese it is foxing.

words.meaning: The teaching; the way things are
words.usage: What the Buddha taught, and also any single thing or event.
Monks, nuns and lay people who practise together. One of the three refuges.
A text presented as the Buddha’s speech. Mahayana sutras were written down from about the first century BCE.

words.meaning: The one who hears the cries of the world
words.usage: The bodhisattva of compassion, Avalokiteshvara, loved across East Asia. Kannon in Japan, Gwaneum in Korea, Quan Am in Vietnam.
The Buddha of Infinite Light. In China his name is also an everyday greeting among Buddhists.
Reciting the name of Amitabha. Nembutsu in Japanese. The main practice of the Pure Land schools.
A realm made by a buddha’s vows where awakening is easy. Amitabha’s is in the west.
The everyday Chinese word, used for Guanyin and as a term of respect.
The Chinese meditation school, from the Sanskrit dhyana. It became Seon in Korea, Thien in Vietnam and Zen in Japan.
The good that comes of good action. In the Mahayana it is given away at once to all beings.
The short verse at the end of any practice that turns its benefit toward everyone.
Tracing or writing out a sutra by hand as a practice. Many Japanese temples offer it to visitors.
Ksitigarbha, who vowed not to rest until the hells are empty. The roadside guardian of travellers and children in Japan.
The gesture of greeting, thanks and respect. Hezhang in Chinese.
The mark of leaving home to become a monk or nun.
The respectful Korean title for a monastic of either sex.
The silent monastic meal eaten from four nested bowls, in which nothing is wasted and the bowls are rinsed and drunk.
The meat-free diet kept by Chinese monastics and by many lay people on set days.
Everything arises from conditions and passes when they pass. The reasoning behind emptiness.

practices.name: The morning vow
practices.instructions: Before you look at a screen, sit up and put your palms together. Call to mind the people and creatures you will meet today, including the ones you would prefer to avoid. Say, aloud or silently: may what I do today be of use to them. Then begin the day. The rule of this Onda is to start the day for others.
practices.why: The bodhisattva’s aim is to wake up for the sake of everyone. A short vow at dawn turns the day from a private project into a shared one.
variations: Write the vow on a card and put it by the bed.
Name three people you will meet today.
Say it with a hand on the heart.

practices.name: One perfection a day
practices.instructions: Take the six perfections in order, one a day, and begin again on the seventh: giving, ethical care, patience, energy, meditation and wisdom. In the morning decide on one concrete way to practise today’s. On a giving day, give something away. On a patience day, wait without sighing. At night, check what happened.
practices.why: The six paramitas are the bodhisattva’s training in Mahayana. Taking one a day makes a big ideal into a practical task.
variations: Write today’s perfection on your hand.
Share today’s with a friend.
Choose the one you find hardest and give it two days.

practices.name: Wake up and smile
practices.instructions: As you wake, before moving, take three slow breaths. On the third out-breath, smile gently and say quietly, as Thich Nhat Hanh teaches: waking up this morning, I smile; twenty-four brand new hours are before me. Then get up. The smile does not need a reason, and it helps to begin the day lightly.
practices.why: This waking verse is one of Thich Nhat Hanh’s short poems for daily life, taught to lay people everywhere. It is a gentle way to begin.
variations: Say it when you open the curtains.
Smile at your face in the bathroom mirror.
Smile at the first person you meet.

practices.name: A bow to the day
practices.instructions: Stand by a window or door, put your palms together and make a slow bow from the waist to the morning, to the street, to all the beings starting their day. Bow three times, slowly, with a breath for each. In East Asian Buddhism the bow is a gesture of respect and thanks, and one does not need to believe anything to make it.
practices.why: Bowing is a common daily act across East Asia, used for greeting, thanking and honouring. Three bows to the day is a quiet start.
variations: Bow to a plant or a tree.
Bow to your family members as they wake.
Bow to the food before you eat.

practices.name: A cup of water offered
practices.instructions: Fill a clean cup with fresh water, set it on a shelf or sill, and look at it for a moment. In Mahayana homes a bowl of clean water is a simple offering. Say in silence: may all beings have what they need. Leave it through the day, then pour it onto a plant in the evening.
practices.why: Water offerings are among the easiest and oldest, because water is clear and cheap, and everyone can give it. The point is the generosity of the mind.
variations: Offer seven small cups in a row.
Offer a cup of tea to someone else.
Water the garden as the offering.

practices.name: Walk to the door as if it mattered
practices.instructions: On your way out of the house, walk the last ten steps slowly, feeling each foot touch the floor, and stop at the door. Breathe once. Step through. In Zen and Pure Land temples, even walking to the hall is done with attention. Make your threshold a place where you arrive.
practices.why: Walking with attention is a Mahayana practice taught by many teachers. A short walk to the door is easy to remember every day.
variations: Do it at every door today.
Say thank you as you pass through.
Count ten steps from the bed to the kitchen.

practices.name: Exchanging self and other
practices.instructions: Sit quietly and bring to mind someone you find difficult. For a few minutes imagine their day from the inside: what they woke up to, what they fear, what they are trying to protect. Notice that they want to be happy and to avoid pain, as you do. Then wish them well, once, in a sentence. Return to your day.
practices.why: Shantideva taught exchanging self and other as a way of making compassion practical. Looking at a difficult person as a fellow sufferer is a powerful and gentle change.
variations: Do it for a stranger you saw this morning.
Do it for someone you love and take them for granted.
Write the sentence of well-wishing on a note and keep it.

practices.name: Give something away
practices.instructions: Give something away today, to someone who will use it. A book from your shelf, a coat, a meal, fifteen minutes of full attention. Give it without a hint of keeping score. The first perfection is giving. The rule of this Onda is to give something every day, and a gift that is a little hard to part with is worth more.
practices.why: Dana, giving, is the first of the six perfections. It loosens the habit of clinging and makes generosity a daily skill.
variations: Give something anonymously.
Give your time instead of an object.
Give a compliment that you really mean.

practices.name: Meet anger with patience
practices.instructions: The next time you feel irritation today, stop for three breaths before you speak. Notice where it sits in the body. Ask: what is this person afraid of? Then say or do the calm thing. Kshanti, patience, is the perfection that Shantideva praised above all. Meet anger with patience once today, deliberately.
practices.why: Shantideva wrote that nothing is evil like hatred and nothing is as hard to bear as patience, and that the one who practises it is happy. Even one pause is a step.
variations: Count to ten in the line at the shop.
Take a pause before replying to a message.
Thank someone who tested you.

practices.name: Speak no ill
practices.instructions: For the next three hours, say nothing negative about anyone who is not present. If you slip, stop, note it and go on. When you must speak of a problem, speak of the facts and not the person. Right speech is a part of the path across Buddhism, and the rule of this Onda is to speak no ill of anyone.
practices.why: Right speech, one of the elements of the Eightfold Path, is taken seriously in Mahayana. A short period of kind speech shows how often we reach for criticism.
variations: Say something good about an absent person.
Keep a tally of slips.
Be silent for ten minutes after a slip.

practices.name: Trace your lunch
practices.instructions: Before you eat, look at your food and trace where it came from: the cook, the shop, the lorry driver, the farmer, the rain, the sun, the soil. Count at least ten links. This is interdependence, a central idea of Mahayana. Then eat the first few bites in silence. Thank those you have named.
practices.why: Thich Nhat Hanh calls this seeing the cloud in the sheet of paper. Tracing a meal back to its sources makes gratitude real.
variations: Do it with a cup of tea.
Do it with a piece of clothing.
Draw the chain on paper.

practices.name: A walking meditation
practices.instructions: Walk slowly in a quiet place, a corridor, a park path or a garden, for fifteen minutes. Breathe in as you take one or two steps, and breathe out as you take two or three. Feel each foot arrive. If you want a thought, let it be: I have arrived, I am home. Walking meditation is taught by Zen and Pure Land teachers alike.
practices.why: Walking meditation is a mainstay of East Asian Buddhist practice, often between periods of sitting. It brings attention into the ordinary act of walking.
variations: Walk barefoot on grass.
Walk in a loop of ten steps.
Walk with a friend, silently.

practices.name: Copying the Heart Sutra
practices.instructions: Take paper, a good pen and an English version of the Heart Sutra, which is about a page long. Sit upright. Copy it out slowly by hand, one line at a time, a few lines each evening. Do not hurry and do not try to work out the meaning. Let the hand and breath move together. When you finish the page, begin again.
practices.why: Copying sutras, shakyo in Japan, is a long-standing practice of devotion and calm in East Asia. The Heart Sutra, the shortest of the great texts, is the most copied.
variations: Copy in the evening light with a brush pen.
Copy a verse of the Way of the Bodhisattva instead.
Copy only one line and think about it.

practices.name: Giving the day away
practices.instructions: Before sleep, recall whatever good came of the day: a kindness done, an effort made, a moment of patience. However small it was, give it away. Say: may any good in this day go to all beings, and may they be free from suffering. Then sleep. The rule of this Onda is to give the merit away at night.
practices.why: Dedication of merit ends every Mahayana practice. Giving the good away keeps it from turning into pride and spreads it to everyone.
variations: Name three specific people in the dedication.
Write the day’s good in one line.
Dedicate the day to someone who is ill.

practices.name: The five contemplations
practices.instructions: Before the evening meal, pause and say the five contemplations in your own words: this food is the gift of earth, sky and many people’s work; may I eat with mindfulness and gratitude; may I eat moderately; may this food give me strength to help others; I receive it for the sake of the path. Then eat slowly, without screens.
practices.why: The five contemplations are said before meals in many Zen and Pure Land temples. They turn eating into an act of appreciation.
variations: Say them silently with palms together.
Eat the first three bites without talking.
Wash up as an act of care.

practices.name: Listen to a chant
practices.instructions: Play a recording of the Great Compassion Mantra, the Heart Sutra or Namo Amituofo, chanted by monks, and sit with your eyes closed for ten minutes. You do not need to follow the words. Let the sound wash through. Chanting is a daily practice in East Asian temples, and listening is a restful way to join.
practices.why: Chanting is central to Mahayana practice. The rhythm and the many voices create a calm that is hard to find by effort alone.
variations: Chant softly along with it.
Listen with the lights off.
Listen while doing nothing else.

practices.name: A thank-you for a helper
practices.instructions: Write a short note to someone who helped you this week, even in a small way: a colleague, a neighbour, a cashier, a family member. Say specifically what they did and how it helped. Send or deliver it. Nothing arises on its own, and a thank you honours the web of help that holds a day together.
practices.why: Gratitude is a form of seeing interdependence. Mahayana teaching holds that every good thing depends on countless causes, and thanking those causes is natural.
variations: Thank someone you have never thanked.
Thank a teacher.
Thank a person in a public role.

practices.name: Incense and a bow
practices.instructions: Light a single stick of incense in a safe holder, away from anything that burns, and stand quietly while the smoke rises. Put your palms together and bow once. Let the scent say that the day is closing. Put the stick out when it is done, and never leave it unattended. If you prefer, light a candle instead.
practices.why: Offering incense is a simple act in East Asian temples and homes. It marks a moment and settles the mind.
variations: Use a candle if you are sensitive to smoke.
Sit for two minutes before it burns down.
Do it by an open window.

practices.name: A temple-style vegetarian meal
practices.instructions: Cook a meal in the spirit of shojin ryori, the Japanese temple cuisine: a small bowl of rice, a clear soup, sesame tofu or simmered vegetables, a pickle and tea. Use seasonal vegetables and cook plainly. Serve it to a friend in small bowls. Say the five contemplations before eating, and eat slowly in near silence.
practices.why: Temple food is built on seasonal vegetables and restraint, to nourish without excess. Cooking and eating it with care is a form of practice in itself.
variations: Cook with a friend and divide the tasks.
Use only five ingredients.
Eat with chopsticks, slowly.

practices.name: A half day of quiet
practices.instructions: Set aside a half day for quiet. Turn off the phone. Sit for twenty minutes, walk for twenty, copy a page of text, drink tea, and sit again. Speak only if needed. Eat simply. Zen and Pure Land retreats are built on this rhythm. Notice what your mind does when there is nothing to do, and end with a dedication.
practices.why: Short retreats are a mainstay of lay Buddhist life across East Asia. A half day at home gives a taste of the rhythm without any commitment.
variations: Do it in a park or garden.
Do it with a friend, in shared silence.
Finish with a long walk.

immersePlan.name: Read a chapter of the Way of the Bodhisattva
immersePlan.text: Read the chapter on patience from Shantideva’s eighth-century poem, or any chapter that calls to you. Choose one verse to carry through the day.

immersePlan.name: Read the Heart Sutra
immersePlan.text: Read the shortest of the great Mahayana texts, a page long, in Red Pine’s translation with commentary. Read it twice, once for sound and once for sense.

immersePlan.name: Read Thich Nhat Hanh
immersePlan.text: Read a chapter of Thich Nhat Hanh’s plain account of the basic teachings, such as the one on mindful breathing or on the four noble truths.

immersePlan.name: Watch Spring, Summer, Fall, Winter... and Spring
immersePlan.text: Watch Kim Ki-duk’s film of a monk and a boy in a floating hermitage on a lake, through the seasons of a life. Notice how little is said.

immersePlan.name: Watch Walk With Me
immersePlan.text: Watch the quiet documentary on the community of Plum Village and Thich Nhat Hanh. Watch how they walk, eat and wait.

immersePlan.name: Watch Departures
immersePlan.text: Watch Yojiro Takita’s film about a cellist who becomes a ritual undertaker, preparing the dead for the coffin with great care. It is gentle and funny and moving.

immersePlan.name: Listen to the Great Compassion Mantra
immersePlan.text: Play the long dharani of Guanyin, chanted by Chinese monastic voices. Let the rhythm roll over you, and join in softly if you wish.

immersePlan.name: Listen to the Heart Sutra chant
immersePlan.text: Play the chanted Heart Sutra by Korean Seon monks. Listen to the wooden fish keeping time. Try to chant along with the first line.

immersePlan.name: Listen to shomyo
immersePlan.text: Play the slow, unaccompanied chanting of Japanese Tendai and Shingon monks. Notice how the voices glide and hold. It is among the oldest living music in Japan.

immersePlan.name: Look at the Water-Moon Avalokiteshvara
immersePlan.text: Look at the Goryeo painting of the bodhisattva of compassion seated by the water, in a thin gauze robe. Find the moon in the painting and the boy at the bottom.

immersePlan.name: Look at Seokguram
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of the granite Buddha in his domed grotto in Gyeongju, built in the eighth century. Notice the calm in the face.

immersePlan.name: Look at the Amida of the Phoenix Hall
immersePlan.text: Look at the gilded Amida of 1053 seated in the Phoenix Hall at Uji, surrounded by carved clouds and flying figures. Imagine the hall lit by candles.

immersePlan.name: Cook Buddha’s delight
immersePlan.text: Stir-fry or braise tofu skin, mushrooms, wood ear, lily buds and cabbage with soy sauce. It is a vegetarian dish traditionally eaten at the Lunar New Year.

immersePlan.name: Eat a Korean temple meal
immersePlan.text: Make a simple meal of rice, seasonal greens, fermented sauces and a bowl of soup, in the spirit of Korean monastery cooking. Eat slowly and leave no food.

immersePlan.name: Cook a pot of congee
immersePlan.text: Simmer rice in plenty of water for an hour until it breaks down into a soft porridge. Serve with ginger, scallions and a drop of sesame oil. It is the comfort food of East Asia.

immersePlan.name: Brew a cup of green tea with attention
immersePlan.text: Use loose leaf and water just off the boil. Watch the leaves unfurl, smell the steam and drink slowly. Tea and Chan have gone together since the Tang dynasty.

immersePlan.name: Brew lotus leaf tea
immersePlan.text: Steep a few dried lotus leaves in hot water and drink it warm. It has a light, grassy taste. The lotus is a symbol of rising clean from mud.

immersePlan.name: Drink barley tea
immersePlan.text: Steep roasted barley, hot in winter or cold in summer. It is the ordinary drink of Korean and Japanese homes, with a nutty, toasty taste.

immersePlan.name: Greet with palms together
immersePlan.text: Greet people today with palms together at the heart and a small bow, the gesture for hello, thank you and sorry across Buddhist Asia.

immersePlan.name: Say the five contemplations before eating
immersePlan.text: Before your next meal, pause and say the five contemplations in your own words. Then eat the first few bites in silence.

immersePlan.name: Offer a stick of incense
immersePlan.text: Light one stick of incense in a safe holder, hold it to the forehead for a moment, and place it upright. Stay while the smoke rises, then put it out safely.

immersePlan.name: Play a game of Go
immersePlan.text: Play a short game of Go on a small board. The stones are placed to surround, not capture, and the game is a conversation. Play with a friend or a program.

immersePlan.name: Play Seongbuldo
immersePlan.text: Play the Korean board game in which pieces climb from hell to the Buddha’s paradise by good deeds and virtue. Play it with dice and a printed board, or draw your own.

immersePlan.name: Play a Journey to the West game
immersePlan.text: Play or read a section of the monkey king’s journey with the monk Xuanzang to fetch the scriptures. Tell one adventure in your own words.

immersePlan.name: Mark Buddha’s Birthday
immersePlan.text: The Buddha’s birthday falls on the eighth day of the fourth lunar month. Pour water gently over a small figure or a flower and make a wish for all beings.

immersePlan.name: Look up the Mogao Caves
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of the cave temples near Dunhuang, painted over a thousand years along the Silk Road. Pick one wall and look for ten minutes.

immersePlan.name: Look up Plum Village
immersePlan.text: Look at the Dordogne community founded by Thich Nhat Hanh. Read about its day, with bells that call everyone to stop and breathe.

immersePlan.name: Practise karuna
immersePlan.text: Karuna is compassion, the wish that others be free from suffering. Today, when you see someone struggling, make that wish silently for them.

immersePlan.name: Practise kshanti
immersePlan.text: Kshanti is patience, one of the six perfections. Choose one thing that will test you today and decide to meet it without hurry or complaint.

immersePlan.name: Practise gassho
immersePlan.text: Gassho is the Japanese gesture of palms together and a slight bow. Use it once today to say thank you, and notice what it does to your face.

rules.why: Before anything else, set the intention that today’s work will be of use to someone besides you.

rules.text: Take no life and eat no meat
rules.why: East Asian Buddhism keeps a vegetarian table. Hold to it for the length of the Onda, and step around the small creatures too.
An object, a meal, your time, your attention or reassurance to someone afraid. Giving is the first training.
When the heat rises, wait for ten breaths before you answer. One held temper counts as the day’s practice.
No blaming, no gossip, no praising yourself at another’s cost. This is among the bodhisattva precepts.

rules.text: Give the merit away at night
rules.why: Whatever good was done, dedicate it to all beings before you sleep. Keep nothing back.

read.title: The Way of the Bodhisattva
read.creator: Shantideva, trans. Padmakara Translation Group
read.why: The handbook of the bodhisattva path in verse, written by an Indian monk at Nalanda. Chapter 6 on patience and chapter 8 on exchanging self and other are the heart.

read.title: The Heart Sutra
read.creator: trans. Red Pine
read.why: Two hundred and sixty Chinese characters that deny every category of Buddhist thought and are chanted daily across East Asia. Red Pine’s commentary goes line by line.

read.title: The Lotus Sutra
read.creator: trans. Burton Watson
read.why: Parables of a burning house, a lost son and a hidden jewel, all saying that everyone will become a buddha. The most loved scripture in East Asia.

read.title: The Vimalakirti Sutra
read.creator: trans. Burton Watson
read.why: A wealthy householder outwits the Buddha’s greatest disciples from his sickbed. Funny, and the charter for lay practice.

read.title: The Three Pure Land Sutras
read.creator: trans. Hisao Inagaki
read.why: The vows of Amitabha and the description of his land. The scriptural basis of the most widely practised Buddhism in the world.

read.title: The Heart of the Buddha’s Teaching
read.creator: Thich Nhat Hanh
read.why: A Vietnamese Zen master sets out the whole teaching in plain words, with the Mahayana reading of each part.

watch.title: Spring, Summer, Fall, Winter... and Spring
watch.creator: Kim Ki-duk
watch.why: A monk and a boy on a floating temple in a Korean lake, through the seasons of a life. Karma shown and never explained.

watch.title: Why Has Bodhi-Dharma Left for the East?
watch.creator: Bae Yong-kyun
watch.why: An old monk, a young monk and an orphan in a mountain hermitage. Slow, exact and very beautiful.

watch.title: Walk With Me
watch.creator: Marc J. Francis and Max Pugh
watch.why: A year inside Plum Village, Thich Nhat Hanh’s monastery in France, with almost no commentary.

watch.title: Departures
watch.creator: Yojiro Takita
watch.why: A cellist becomes an encoffiner in rural Japan. A warm film about the Buddhist funeral and care for the dead.

listen.title: The Great Compassion Mantra
listen.creator: Chinese monastic chanting; many recordings
listen.why: The Dabei Zhou, eighty-four phrases addressed to Guanyin, chanted to a wooden fish drum in temples every morning.

listen.title: Heart Sutra
listen.creator: Korean Seon monastic chant
listen.why: The Banya Simgyeong, driven by the moktak, the hollow wooden clapper. Listen for the mantra at the end.

listen.title: Namo Amituofo
listen.creator: Pure Land recitation; many recordings
listen.why: Four or six syllables repeated for hours in a slow, rising melody. The sound of ordinary Chinese Buddhism.

listen.title: Shomyo: Buddhist Ritual Chant
listen.creator: Monks of Japanese Tendai and Shingon temples
listen.why: Long sliding vocal lines brought from Tang China in the ninth century. One of the oldest living vocal traditions.

art.title: Water-Moon Avalokiteshvara
art.creator: Goryeo court painters, Korea
art.why: Guanyin sits on a rock by the sea under a full moon, in gold line on silk so fine the veil is see-through. About 160 survive, in Seoul, Tokyo, New York and elsewhere.

art.title: The Leshan Giant Buddha
art.creator: Sichuan, China
art.why: A seated Maitreya seventy-one metres high carved from a river cliff, begun by a monk who hoped it would calm the waters.

art.title: Seokguram Grotto
art.creator: Gyeongju, South Korea
art.why: A granite Buddha in a domed chamber on a mountain, facing the sunrise over the East Sea. Among the finest sculpture in Asia.

art.title: Amida Buddha of the Phoenix Hall
art.creator: Jocho; Byodo-in, Uji, Japan
art.why: A gilded Amitabha in a hall built to look like his palace in the Pure Land, reflected in a pond. It is on the ten-yen coin.

eat.title: Buddha’s delight (luohan zhai)
eat.creator: Tofu skin, mushrooms, wood ear, cabbage and glass noodles braised together
eat.why: The best known dish of Chinese temple cooking, eaten in many homes on the first day of the new year.

eat.title: Korean temple food
eat.creator: Seasonal greens, fermented soybean paste, rice and soup
eat.why: No meat and none of the five pungent plants, such as garlic and onion, which are said to disturb the mind. Jeong Kwan made it famous.

eat.title: Shojin ryori
eat.creator: Sesame tofu, simmered vegetables, pickles, rice and miso soup
eat.why: Japanese devotion cuisine: small dishes in five colours and five tastes, nothing wasted.

eat.title: Congee
eat.creator: Rice simmered with plenty of water until it breaks down
eat.why: The morning meal of Chinese monasteries, praised in the monastic codes for ten benefits.

drink.title: Green tea
drink.creator: Loose leaf, water just off the boil
drink.why: Tea and Chan grew up together in the mountains of China. Monks drank it to stay awake in meditation.

drink.title: Lotus leaf tea
drink.creator: Dried lotus leaf steeped in hot water
drink.why: A Korean temple drink, mild and faintly sweet. The lotus grows from mud without being stained by it.

drink.title: Barley tea
drink.creator: Roasted barley, hot or cold
drink.why: The everyday drink of Korea and Japan, with no caffeine, served with temple meals.

customs.title: Palms together
customs.creator: The greeting and the thanks
customs.why: A slight bow with joined hands when meeting a monastic, entering a hall or receiving food.

customs.title: Three bows
customs.creator: To the Buddha, the teaching and the community
customs.why: On entering a main hall, people bow three times to the floor. Visitors may simply stand quietly or bow from the waist.

customs.title: Offering incense
customs.creator: One stick or three, held to the forehead
customs.why: Lit, raised with both hands and placed upright in the burner. The fragrance stands for conduct that benefits everyone around.

customs.title: The five contemplations
customs.creator: Before eating
customs.why: A short reflection on where the food came from, whether one has earned it, and why one eats: to sustain the body for practice.

games.title: Go (weiqi, baduk)
games.creator: Board game · China
games.why: Black and white stones on a grid. Loved by monks and scholars across East Asia as a lesson in balance, patience and letting go of small gains.

games.title: Table of Buddhist Promotion (Seongbuldo)
games.creator: Board game · Korea
games.why: A dice game on a chart of the realms of rebirth, from the hells up to buddhahood, played in Korean temples at new year. Players chant as they roll.

games.title: Journey to the West
games.creator: Novel and many game adaptations, including Black Myth: Wukong (2024)
games.why: The Monkey King escorts a monk to India to fetch the sutras. The games are action spectacles, but the tale underneath is a Buddhist pilgrimage.

festivals.title: Buddha’s Birthday
festivals.creator: 8th day of the 4th lunar month, April or May
festivals.why: Lantern parades in Korea, bathing a small statue of the infant Buddha with sweet tea in China and Japan.

festivals.title: Ullambana, the Ghost Festival
festivals.creator: 15th day of the 7th lunar month, August
festivals.why: Offerings for ancestors and all hungry spirits. Obon in Japan, with dances and lanterns floated on water.

festivals.title: Guanyin’s days
festivals.creator: 19th of the 2nd, 6th and 9th lunar months
festivals.why: Her birth, awakening and leaving home. Temples are crowded and many people eat vegetarian.

festivals.title: Bodhi Day
festivals.creator: 8th day of the 12th lunar month; 8 December in Japan
festivals.why: The Buddha’s awakening. Chinese families cook laba congee with eight kinds of grain and fruit.

places.title: Mount Putuo
places.creator: Zhejiang, China
places.why: An island of temples sacred to Guanyin, reached by ferry. One of the four holy mountains of Chinese Buddhism.

places.title: Haeinsa
places.creator: South Gyeongsang, South Korea
places.why: A mountain monastery that keeps the Tripitaka Koreana: the whole canon carved on more than eighty thousand wooden blocks in the thirteenth century. Temple stays are offered.

places.title: Todai-ji
places.creator: Nara, Japan
places.why: A sixteen-metre bronze Buddha of the eighth century inside one of the largest wooden buildings in the world.

places.title: The Mogao Caves
places.creator: Dunhuang, Gansu, China
places.why: Nearly five hundred painted cave temples on the Silk Road, made over a thousand years. Book ahead, since visitor numbers are limited.

places.title: Plum Village
places.creator: Dordogne, France
places.why: The monastery founded by Thich Nhat Hanh in 1982. Lay people can join retreats and days of mindfulness.

ethics.title: Compassion in action
ethics.text: Compassion is counted as the root of the whole path. It is measured by what it does: staying with those who suffer and working to relieve them.
ethics.practice: Do one thing today for someone who is suffering, even if it is only to sit with them.

ethics.title: Giving
ethics.text: The bodhisattva gives things, gives protection from fear and gives the teaching. The best gift is made with no thought of giver, gift or receiver.
ethics.practice: Give something today and tell no one.

ethics.title: Patience
ethics.text: Anger burns up good faster than anything. Shantideva says an enemy is as useful as a treasure found at home, because only an enemy lets you practise patience.
ethics.practice: Thank someone who irritated you today, silently, for the practice.

ethics.title: Not harming
ethics.text: The first precept is to take no life. In East Asia this became a vegetarian table and the custom of freeing animals bound for slaughter.
ethics.practice: Eat nothing today that was killed for you.

ethics.title: Truthful and kind speech
ethics.text: The bodhisattva precepts forbid lying, slander, praising oneself and putting down others. Speech should be true, timely and of benefit.
ethics.practice: Catch one unkind remark before it leaves your mouth.

ethics.title: Equality of self and other
ethics.text: My suffering matters to me only because it is mine. Seen from outside, everyone’s weighs the same. Ethics begins from that view.
ethics.practice: Give a stranger’s inconvenience the same weight as your own, once.

philosophy.title: The bodhisattva vow
philosophy.text: Earlier Buddhism aimed at one’s own release. The Mahayana held up a larger aim: to become a buddha so as to free everyone, however long it takes. The vow is absurdly large on purpose.
philosophy.practice: State one aim for your life that is not about you.

philosophy.title: Emptiness
philosophy.text: Look for the thing in itself and you find parts, causes and a name. A cup is clay, fire, a potter and a use. It is real, it holds tea, and it has no core apart from all that. So with a self.
philosophy.practice: Pick one object and trace five things it depends on to exist.

philosophy.title: Wisdom and compassion
philosophy.text: They are called the two wings of a bird. Wisdom without compassion is cold, and compassion without wisdom is blind and soon exhausted. Each trains the other.
philosophy.practice: In one decision today ask both questions: what is true here, and what is kind.

philosophy.title: Skilful means
philosophy.text: The Lotus Sutra tells of a father who lures his children from a burning house by promising toys. A teaching is judged by whether it helps. There are as many doors as there are people.
philosophy.practice: Help someone today in the way they need, which may not be the way you prefer.

philosophy.title: Buddha nature
philosophy.text: Every being already has what it takes to awaken, as a seed has the tree. Practice uncovers this capacity. East Asian Buddhism builds its confidence on the idea.
philosophy.practice: Treat one person today as someone who will certainly become wise.

philosophy.title: Interbeing
philosophy.text: Thich Nhat Hanh’s word for dependent arising. In a sheet of paper there is a cloud, rain, a tree and a logger. Nothing stands alone, and so nothing is beneath concern.
philosophy.practice: Before one meal, name five beings who made it possible.

philosophy.title: Samsara is nirvana
philosophy.text: Nagarjuna argued that there is no line between the troubled world and peace. Freedom is this same life, seen without grasping. So the bodhisattva has no reason to leave.
philosophy.practice: Find one ordinary, tedious moment today and give it your whole attention.

philosophy.title: Other-power
philosophy.text: The Pure Land schools teach that in a hard age few can free themselves by effort. One relies on the vow of Amitabha, and practice becomes an expression of gratitude.
philosophy.practice: Notice one thing today that you received and could never have earned.

journal: Whose suffering did you step toward today?
What did you give, and what did you hold back?
When did anger rise, and what did you do with it?
Who did you find difficult, and what might their day have been like?
What does your morning vow actually commit you to?
What exists by itself?
Where did you put yourself first without noticing?
What did you eat today, and who made it possible?
Which of the six perfections is weakest in you?
What would you do if you were certain everyone could awaken?
Where were you kind without being wise?
Where were you right without being kind?
What are you storing up that you could give away?
Who heard your cries when you needed it?
Whose cries do you not want to hear?
What did copying the sutra do to your mind?
What merit, however small, can you dedicate tonight?
What is the self you are defending?
What help did you offer in your way and not in theirs?
What have you received that you could never repay?
Where did you waste something today?
What grudge could you release?
What would patience have looked like?
Which creature did you step around?
What ordinary moment was complete?
What does emptiness take away from you, and what does it give?
Who is your enemy, and what are they teaching you?
How large could your aim be?
What do you still want only for yourself?
For as long as space endures: what will you stay for?
reflect: What changed when you began each day for others?
Which perfection grew, and which resisted?
Whom do you see differently after exchanging places with them?
What did giving away the merit each night do?
What does emptiness mean to you now, in your own words?
Which vow will you carry forward?

intro: About four centuries after the Buddha’s death, new scriptures began to circulate among Buddhist monks and nuns in India. They praised a figure called the bodhisattva: a person who vows to become a fully awakened buddha, over as many lifetimes as it takes, in order to free every living being. The movement that grew around these texts called itself the Mahayana, the Great Vehicle. It is the Buddhism of China, Korea, Japan, Vietnam, Tibet and Mongolia, and of more than half the world’s Buddhists.

Two ideas carry it. The first is compassion without limit. A bodhisattva does not leave the world for a private peace but stays, and the vow is renewed every morning: beings are numberless, I vow to save them. The second is emptiness. The Perfection of Wisdom sutras and the philosopher Nagarjuna argued that nothing has a fixed nature of its own. Everything arises in dependence on everything else. Far from a bleak teaching, this is what makes change, kindness and awakening possible.

From these roots came many schools. Chan, which became Zen, stressed meditation and direct insight. Pure Land taught reliance on the vow of the Buddha Amitabha and the recitation of his name, and became the faith of most ordinary people. Tiantai and Huayan built vast systems of thought around the Lotus and Flower Garland sutras. The Vajrayana of Tibet is a Mahayana tradition with its own methods. This app has separate Ondas for Zen and for Tibetan Buddhism. This one keeps to the common ground beneath them.

That common ground is practical. It is the six perfections: giving, ethical care, patience, energy, meditation and wisdom. It is devotion to Guanyin, who hears the cries of the world, and to Earth Store, who will not rest until the hells are empty. It is vegetarian food, incense, bows, the copying of sutras, and the habit of giving away the merit of every good act as soon as it is done.

In this Onda you will set a vow each morning, take one perfection each day, practise exchanging yourself with someone difficult, copy the Heart Sutra by hand and dedicate the day before sleep. You are a guest. Taking refuge and receiving the bodhisattva precepts are formal steps made with a teacher and a community, and nothing here stands in for them.

One caution about a word. Mahayana texts sometimes call earlier Buddhism the Hinayana, the lesser vehicle. The term is a polemic and is not used for the living Theravada tradition, which has its own Onda here.
guide.origin: India, then China, Korea, Japan, Vietnam and the Himalayas
guide.era: Mahayana sutras appear from about the 1st century BCE. It is the majority form of Buddhism today

figures.name: Nagarjuna
figures.bio: The Indian philosopher of the middle way, who argued in tight verse that all things are empty of a nature of their own. Nearly every Mahayana school claims him.

figures.name: Asanga and Vasubandhu
figures.bio: Half-brothers from Gandhara who founded the Yogachara school, a close study of how the mind builds its world.

figures.name: Kumarajiva
figures.bio: A monk from Kucha on the Silk Road, taken to China as a captive, whose translations of the Lotus, Diamond and Vimalakirti sutras are still the ones chanted.

figures.name: Zhiyi
figures.bio: Founder of the Tiantai school on a mountain in Zhejiang. He ordered the whole of Buddhist teaching around the Lotus Sutra and wrote great manuals of meditation.

figures.name: Xuanzang
figures.bio: A Chinese monk who walked to India and back, a journey of seventeen years, and returned with hundreds of texts. His version of the Heart Sutra is the standard one.

figures.name: Shantideva
figures.bio: A monk of Nalanda university. Legend says his fellows thought him lazy until he recited The Way of the Bodhisattva and rose into the air.

figures.name: Wonhyo
figures.bio: The most loved Korean monk, who gave up his robes, sang and danced the teaching through villages and wrote some eighty works reconciling the schools.

figures.name: Shinran
figures.bio: A Japanese monk who married, called himself neither monk nor layman and taught complete trust in Amitabha’s vow. His school is the largest in Japan.

figures.name: Thich Nhat Hanh
figures.bio: A Vietnamese Zen master exiled for opposing the war. He taught mindfulness and engaged Buddhism worldwide from Plum Village in France.

history.detail: Siddhartha Gautama awakens under a tree at Bodh Gaya and teaches for some forty-five years across the plain of the Ganges.
The Perfection of Wisdom texts begin to circulate in writing. Their origin is debated. They may have arisen among forest monks and in several places at once.
Monks and merchants carry texts and images along the Silk Road. The first translations into Chinese are made at Luoyang.
His Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way give the Mahayana its philosophy of emptiness.
Buddhism is brought to the Korean kingdom of Goguryeo in 372, and from Baekje to the Japanese court in the middle of the sixth century.
With a team of hundreds he produces clear, beautiful Chinese versions of the main sutras. Chinese Buddhism can now think in its own language.
Tiantai, Huayan, Pure Land and Chan take shape. Monasteries become the largest landowners and centres of learning in the empire.
The emperor Wuzong closes thousands of monasteries and returns a quarter of a million monks and nuns to lay life. Chan and Pure Land, which need few books and buildings, survive best.
A copy found at Dunhuang is the oldest dated printed book in the world. It was made for free distribution, to earn merit for the donor’s parents.
With the Mongols invading, the Goryeo court has the entire canon carved on more than eighty thousand woodblocks. They are still kept at Haeinsa.
Honen and Shinran teach the Pure Land path, Eisai and Dogen bring Zen, and Nichiren preaches the Lotus Sutra. All three movements still thrive.
Buddhism is suppressed in China during the Cultural Revolution and revives afterward. Reformers such as Taixu and movements such as Fo Guang Shan and Tzu Chi in Taiwan turn it toward social service.
Teachers from Japan, Korea, Vietnam and Taiwan found centres on every continent. Engaged Buddhism links practice to peace work and care for the earth.

concepts.text: One who lives for the awakening of all.
concepts.detail: The ideal person of the Mahayana. The term covers great figures such as Guanyin and Manjushri and also anyone who has made the vow. The path is mapped in ten stages.
The resolve to become a buddha for the sake of others. Teachers distinguish the wish from the active practice, as planning a journey differs from setting out.
Things exist, but only in dependence on causes, parts and naming. Nagarjuna calls this the middle way between saying things truly exist and saying they do not.
Giving, ethics, patience, energy, meditation and wisdom. The first five are called blind without the sixth. Some lists add four more to make ten.

concepts.text: The right help for each person.
concepts.detail: Buddhas teach differently to different hearers, as a doctor prescribes differently for different patients. The Lotus Sutra uses the idea to reconcile all earlier teachings as one vehicle.

concepts.text: The seed of awakening in everyone.
concepts.detail: Taught in the Tathagatagarbha sutras and central in East Asia. It is likened to gold in ore or a statue wrapped in rags.

concepts.text: Three ways a buddha is present.
concepts.detail: The body of truth, which is reality itself; the body of enjoyment, seen in visions and pure lands; and the body of appearance, such as the historical Buddha.
Amitabha vowed to create a land where anyone who calls on him could be reborn and awaken easily. Some take it as a place and some as the purified mind.
Good acts produce benefit. A bodhisattva turns that benefit over to all beings at once, which also guards against pride.

facts.text: The Diamond Sutra of 868, found in a sealed cave at Dunhuang and now in the British Library, is the oldest complete printed book that carries a date.
Guanyin began in India as the male bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara and came to be pictured as a woman in China from about the tenth century.
The laughing fat figure often called the Buddha in the West is Budai, a tenth century Chinese monk regarded as a form of the future buddha Maitreya.
The Heart Sutra is short enough to be printed on a fan or a teacup, and it is.
The Tripitaka Koreana has more than fifty-two million characters and scholars have found almost no errors in it.
Tofu, soy milk and wheat gluten owe much of their development to the kitchens of Chinese monasteries.

glossary.meaning: One who has reached release; the ideal of earlier Buddhism
The bodhisattva of wisdom, shown with a sword
The end of greed, hatred and delusion
The Buddhist canon, literally three baskets

sensitivity.note: Mahayana Buddhism is the living religion of hundreds of millions of people. This Onda offers practices that East Asian traditions share with lay visitors. It is no substitute for taking refuge, receiving precepts or learning from a teacher and a community.
requiredCaveats: Schools differ widely. What is central in Pure Land may be marginal in Chan, and the reverse.
Images of buddhas and bodhisattvas are objects of devotion. Do not use them as decoration, and never place them on the floor.
The word Hinayana is a polemical term. It should not be used for Theravada Buddhists.
Emptiness is easily misheard as nihilism. It is taught alongside compassion for that reason.
